title: Loss functions: what you are actually minimising
story:
A network does not know what you want. It produces numbers, and something has to convert the gap between those numbers and the desired ones into a single value that can be made smaller. That value is the loss, and the choice of how to compute it decides what the network learns — more directly than the architecture does.

Start with why it has to be a single number. Training works by adjusting parameters in whatever direction reduces the loss, and direction only means something with respect to one quantity. Several measures of quality cannot all be improved along one direction, because they will disagree about which way that is. So the loss is a commitment: whatever you care about has to be compressed into one scalar, and anything not in that scalar is not being optimised, however often it is mentioned in the project's goals.

The two standard shapes follow from what kind of answer is wanted.

When the output is a quantity, the natural measure is how far off the prediction is. Squaring that distance before adding it up has a specific consequence worth seeing: an error twice as large contributes four times as much, so the sum is dominated by the worst predictions. That is a choice, not a formality. It makes the network attend to large misses at the expense of small ones, which is right when a large error is disproportionately bad and wrong when a few extreme cases are noise or corrupt data — in which case the network will contort itself to accommodate them.

When the output is a choice between categories, the measure is how much probability the network assigned to the correct one, penalised so that being confidently wrong costs far more than being uncertain. The shape matters here too: assigning almost no probability to what actually happened produces a very large penalty, growing without bound as the assigned probability approaches zero. So a network trained this way learns to avoid confident mistakes more strongly than it learns to be confidently right, and calibration comes out of the loss rather than being added later.

Now the part that is worth more than either formula. The loss is a proxy for what you want, and it is always a lossy one, so the interesting failures are cases where the loss is genuinely minimised and the result is useless.

The clearest example is an uneven distribution of categories. If almost every example belongs to one category, a network that always predicts that category achieves a low loss and has learned nothing. It has not failed; it has succeeded at the thing you asked for, and the thing you asked for was not the thing you wanted. No amount of training fixes this, because training is working correctly. The remedy is to change the loss — weighting the rare category more heavily — or to change the data, and choosing between those is a modelling decision rather than a tuning one.

The general shape of that failure recurs everywhere. Optimising a proxy hard enough finds the places where the proxy and the goal diverge, and a more capable model finds them faster, because capability is precisely the ability to exploit the structure of what it was given. So a loss that was adequate for a small model can become a liability for a large one.

Which yields the habit worth keeping. When a model is performing badly, check what it is being asked to minimise before examining the architecture. And when a model is performing well against its loss and badly in use, do not look for a bug — the loss and the goal have come apart, and the gap between them is the whole problem.

problem.name: The proxy you optimise
problem.shape: A model's output must be turned into one number that training can reduce.
tell: the loss is falling and the model is not more useful
a rare but important category is being predicted almost never
several goals are stated and only one is in the objective
extreme cases are dominating what the model attends to
problem.move: Read what is being minimised before examining anything else, and check that everything you claim to care about appears in it. When performance against the loss and performance in use diverge, treat the loss as the problem rather than looking for a bug.
problem.invariant: Training reduces exactly one number, so anything not represented in the loss is not being optimised — however prominently it appears in the project's goals.
problem.breaks: Optimising a proxy hard enough finds where the proxy and the goal diverge, and a more capable model finds those places faster, because capability is the ability to exploit the structure it was given. So a loss adequate for a small model can become a liability for a large one.

cost.time: compressing several concerns into one scalar forces a weighting decision that is a modelling judgement rather than a tuning parameter
cost.beats: reporting several metrics and not optimising any of them, which is honest and gives training no direction, and optimising each in turn, which improves whichever was last touched

worked.problem: A classifier reaches a very low loss and is useless in practice. What happened?
worked.reasoning:
Most likely the loss was minimised correctly and it was not measuring what you wanted. The clearest version is an uneven distribution of categories.

If almost every example belongs to one category, a network that always predicts that category achieves a low loss while having learned nothing at all. Note what kind of failure that is: the network has not failed. It succeeded at the task it was given, and the task it was given was not the task you wanted. So no amount of further training fixes it, because training is working correctly — which is why this is diagnosed by reading the objective rather than by inspecting the model.

The remedy is to change the loss, by weighting the rare category more heavily, or to change the data. Choosing between those is a modelling decision rather than a tuning one, and it requires knowing what the relative cost of the two kinds of mistake actually is — which is information that lives outside the model entirely.

It is worth understanding why this is structural. Training works by adjusting parameters in whatever direction reduces the loss, and direction only means something with respect to one quantity. Several measures of quality cannot all be improved along a single direction, because they will disagree about which way that is. So the loss is a commitment: everything you care about must be compressed into one scalar, and anything absent from that scalar is not being optimised however often it is mentioned.

The shapes of the standard losses are choices in the same way, and worth knowing for their consequences rather than their formulas. Squaring the distance for a quantitative output means an error twice as large contributes four times as much, so the sum is dominated by the worst predictions — right when a large error is disproportionately bad, wrong when extreme cases are noise, in which case the network contorts itself to accommodate corrupt data. For a choice between categories, penalising low probability assigned to the correct answer grows without bound as that probability approaches zero, so the network learns to avoid confident mistakes more strongly than to be confidently right, and calibration comes out of the loss rather than being added afterwards.

The general pattern I would name explicitly, because it extends well past this case: optimising a proxy hard enough finds the places where the proxy and the goal diverge, and a more capable model finds them faster, since capability is precisely the ability to exploit the structure of what it was given. A loss that was adequate for a small model can therefore become a liability for a large one, which means the objective needs revisiting when capability increases, not only when performance drops.

So the habit is: when a model performs badly, check what it is being asked to minimise before examining the architecture. And when it performs well against its loss and badly in use, do not look for a bug — the loss and the goal have come apart, and that gap is the whole problem.

problem.practice: Take a task you care about and write down everything you want from it, then write the loss. The items on the first list that are absent from the second are the things you are not optimising, and naming them is the point of the exercise.

beats.broke: A network produces numbers and has no idea what is wanted, so without a single quantity to reduce there is no direction for training to move in.
beats.fix: Compress what you want into one scalar the training can minimise, choosing its shape deliberately — squaring distances attends to the worst cases, penalising low probability on the right answer produces calibration.
beats.cost: Anything not in the scalar is not being optimised, so the loss is always a lossy proxy — and the interesting failures are the ones where it is genuinely minimised and the result is useless.

interview.q: A classifier reaches a very low loss and is useless in practice. What happened?
interview.trap: Looking for a bug in the model. The likeliest answer is that training worked perfectly on an objective that did not measure what you wanted — an uneven distribution of categories being the clearest case.
